pronunciation.note: Ugayafukiaezu is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. His strange name refers to a birth hut thatched with cormorant feathers and left unfinished. He is the immediate father of Emperor Jimmu.

domains.title: Cormorant Thatching Unfinished
domains.subtitle: Father of Jimmu and Link Between Sea and Land
domains.lead: Ugayafukiaezu is one of the most strangely named figures in Japanese myth. His name describes the unfinished thatched hut, covered with cormorant feathers, in which he was born. As the son of Hoori and the sea princess Toyotama, and the father of Emperor Jimmu, he is the final link between the ocean depths and the imperial line.

cards.name: Father of Jimmu
cards.desc: His fourth son, Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko, won the succession and founded the Yamato line as Emperor Jimmu (Kojiki I).

cards.name: Sea-Land Bridge
cards.desc: Son of Hoori the land-hunter and Toyotama-bime, daughter of the sea god Watatsumi — the marriage that joined coast and deep.

cards.name: Unfinished Birth Hut
cards.desc: His name glosses the cormorant-feather thatch of the Kojiki's birth hut — and the roof never finished (鵜草葺不合).

cards.name: Imperial Ancestor
cards.desc: The last link of the divine genealogy: through him the regalia line descends to the historic emperors (Nihon Shoki, books 1–3).

symbols.name: Cormorant feathers
symbols.meaning: The black plumage of the diving bird that the Kojiki makes the roof of his birth hut (ugaya)

symbols.name: Thatching
symbols.meaning: fukiaezu — 'not yet completed': the unfinished roof read directly as his name

symbols.name: Sea and land
symbols.meaning: His double heritage: the tide-jewel deep of Watatsumi's house and the hills of his father Hoori

symbols.name: Bow and fishhook
symbols.meaning: The paternal gear of Hoori's line — the hunter's bow against the sea's hooked line

mythology.lead: Ugayafukiaezu's mythology is the final chapter of the Hoori–Toyotama cycle and the prologue to the reign of Jimmu: one night on a seashore, one unfinished roof, one farewell poem, and a lineage that steps out of the hut into history.

myths.title: The Cormorant-Feather Hut
myths.text: The Kojiki (age of gods) tells how the sea princess Toyotama-bime, daughter of Watatsumi the sea god, came up from the deep to bear the child of the land-hunter Hoori. On the seashore she built a hut and thatched its roof with cormorant feathers, and as her hour came she warned her husband: do not look inside. Hoori waited, but when the cry came he could not hold back; he peered through the wall and saw his wife transformed into a great sea-creature — the Kojiki says an eight-fathom shark — coiled in labor. Toyotama knew herself shamed. She left the newborn where he lay, in the hut whose cormorant thatch had never been finished, and the compilers give the child his name from the shelter itself: Ugayafukiaezu, 'Cormorant-Thatching-Unfinished'. The scene survives because a roof was never completed: a goddess of the sea delivering on land, and a lineage beginning in the gap between the elements.

myths.title: The Farewell Song
myths.text: Before she returned to the sea, Toyotama spoke the poem the Kojiki preserves as one of its most celebrated archaic songs: had you not shamed me, I would have come and gone by the sea-road, and for ever eased the way of the ships; but now that you have looked, the crossing will be hard — the precise wording varies in translation, but Philippi's rendering keeps its reproach intact. She left the child in the care of her younger sister Tamayori — 'Good Jewel' — who came up out of the water to suckle him. In a text crowded with genealogies, the poem is the rare moment the myth turns elegy: a mother who could have made the sea a road for her son instead leaves him a song — and the imperial line inherits, with its treasures, a story about the price of looking.

myths.title: The Aunt Who Stayed
myths.text: Tamayori raised the boy of the unfinished hut, and when he was grown the Kojiki says she became his wife; the compilers record the union without comment, the sea line marrying back into itself. Four sons were born: Itsuse, Inahi, Mikeiri, and the youngest, Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko. The Nihon Shoki's parallel account of the succession tells how the three elder brothers marched east against the defiant chiefs of the land and failed — Itsuse fell at Kusaka, his army repulsed — while the youngest, guided by the three-legged crow Yatagarasu sent down from heaven, found the road through the mountains, defeated Nagasunehiko, and planted the Yamato line. The child of the roofless hut becomes the hinge on which the narrative turns from gods to kings: from this point the chronicles stop telling of the divine age and begin, almost, to tell of a realm.

myths.title: The Treasures Cross the Water
myths.text: The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki agree on the cargo of the line Ugayafukiaezu completes: the imperial regalia — the mirror, the sword Kusanagi, and the jewel — descended from Amaterasu with Ninigi, passed down through Hoori's house, and went east with Jimmu on the expedition, the divine mirror and sword carried against the rebels of the land. Later tradition placed the unfinished hut's son at the exact point where the age of the gods closes: everything celestial has now crossed into a single human lineage. The Nihon Shoki's more sober parallel strips away wonders and keeps the genealogy, which is testimony of its own kind — whether read as myth or as charter, the story exists to make one claim: that the family of the unfinished roof was entrusted with heaven's treasures, and did not drop them.

lore.syncretism: Ugayafukiaezu has no cult and no shrine — his whole existence is genealogical, and his meaning is that of the custom his name preserves. Japanese ethnographers documented birth huts, ubuya, in which mothers delivered and secluded themselves, persisting in parts of the country into the twentieth century; the Kojiki's cormorant-feather hut is read against this custom as its mythic charter. Medieval Buddhist exegetes folded the age-of-gods narratives into the honji suijaku framework, treating the kami's doings as local manifestations of cosmic Buddha-activity, while Edo-period nativists of the Kokugaku school — Motoori Norinaga above all — pored over the strange compounds of the divine genealogy as evidence of an authentically Japanese antiquity. Each tradition found in the unfinished roof what it needed: ritualists a birth custom, monks a parable of manifestation, nativists a pure native word.
lore.culturalLegacy: His legacy runs through the one institution he made possible. As Jimmu's father, Ugayafukiaezu stands in the imperial genealogy, and Japan's National Foundation Day (11 February) marks the legendary accession of the son born in the unfinished hut. The birth-hut custom behind his name outlived the myth in practice: ethnographers recorded ubuya seclusion into the modern period, especially in the Izu Islands and the northeast. In scholarship his name is a permanent puzzle — every handbook of Japanese myth pauses over the cormorant feathers — and in popular culture the Jimmu cycle, Yatagarasu and all, returns in anime, manga, and school texts as the nation's prologue. The strange name does the work: a lineage that begins under an unfinished roof can never be accused of having begun too comfortably.
lore.extendedMeditation: He is named for what was never finished. Every other figure of the Kojiki's first books wins a name from a deed, a place, a father; Ugayafukiaezu wins his from defective carpentry — a roof of cormorant feathers, begun in haste and never completed. Scholars have tried to make the name less odd, reading the feathers as ritual paraphernalia, the incompleteness as birth taboo, the whole hut as a lodge built for a single night and deliberately left open to the sky. All may be true, and the text does not care. What matters is that the imperial line — the oldest continuously claimed succession on earth — passes through a child born in a shelter that was never made weatherproof. The unfinished roof is the tradition's quiet joke and its deepest claim at once: origins are not supposed to be comfortable, complete, or safe. Beginnings, like thatch, are provisional; what matters is who carries the story out of the hut.

lore.archaeology: Ugayafukiaezu has no independent material cult; the evidence is textual and funerary. The Kojiki survives through the Shinpukuji manuscript line (supplemented by the 1371–72 date-bearing copies), and the Nihon Shoki through Heian-period manuscript traditions. The imperial mausoleum his line supposedly founded is real as a site: at Kashihara in Nara prefecture the Imperial Household Agency tends Unebi-yama no ushitora no sumi no misasagi, the kofun-style tomb attributed to Jimmu, the son whose birth the hut story explains — a large early-period enclosure, undisturbed by archaeology and unprovenanced to any historical person. Birth huts (ubuya) themselves, the custom behind the myth, persisted in parts of Japan into the twentieth century and were documented by ethnographers — the closest the earth comes to the cormorant-thatched roof.
lore.originalScriptNote: The age-of-gods names are written in kanji that gloss rather than transcribe. The full ceremonial form is 鵜草葺不合命 (Ugayafukiaezu-no-mikoto), with the honorific 命 (mikoto): 鵜 “cormorant,” 草 “grass, reed,” 葺 “to thatch,” 不合 “not joined, unfinished.” The characters record the Kojiki's own explanation of the name, not a phonetic spelling; medieval manuscripts abbreviate the compound variously, and its reading has been debated since the earliest commentaries.
